name: Simulated Annealing
analogy: Think of it as shaking a tray of marbles to find its lowest hollow. At first you shake hard, so marbles hop out of shallow dips; as you shake more gently they settle into the deepest hollow. The shaking strength is the temperature, and it is lowered slowly on a schedule.

steps.title: Start with one solution and a high temperature
steps.description: Unlike a swarm or a population, only one current solution is held. The temperature starts high, which means worse moves are accepted easily.
steps.inExample: The current setting is a 20-bar lookback window and a hold of 12 bars, with a score of 30 net points per day and a starting temperature of 50 points.

steps.title: Propose a small random change
steps.description: Nudge the current solution a little to get a neighbour. The size of the nudge defines how the search wanders through the space.
steps.inExample: The window is nudged to 22 bars and the hold to 11 bars, and the new setting scores 26 points per day, worse by 4 points.

steps.title: Always accept an improvement
steps.description: If the neighbour scores better, move to it at once. The search never turns down a gain.
steps.inExample: A later neighbour of 24 bars and a hold of 10 bars scores 33 points per day and is accepted immediately.

steps.title: Sometimes accept a worse move
steps.description: A worse neighbour is accepted with a chance that depends on how much worse it is and on the temperature. At high temperature the chance is high; at low temperature it is small. This is how the search climbs out of dead ends.
steps.inExample: A move that is worse by 4 points is accepted with about a 92 percent chance when the temperature is 50 points, but only about a 14 percent chance when the temperature has cooled to 2 points.

steps.title: Cool the temperature step by step
steps.description: After a set number of tries the temperature is reduced. The cooling schedule is the most important design choice, because it decides how long the search explores before it settles.
steps.inExample: The temperature keeps 95 percent of itself every 20 tries over 2,000 tries, falling from 50 points to under 1 point.

steps.title: Report the best setting seen
steps.description: When the temperature is near zero, the search behaves like a plain climb. The best solution seen along the whole trail is returned.
steps.inExample: The best setting seen is a 26-bar lookback window and a hold of 9 bars, scoring 38 net points per day.

useFor.example: Searching the lookback window and holding time of an MNQ mean-reversion rule where small changes flip many trades.
Searching sequences of execution steps by swapping two at a time, accepting some worse sequences early on.
Searching continuous weights against a risk-adjusted score with awkward constraints when a single trail is preferred over a swarm.
Exploring which indicators to combine and in what order through small structural edits.

avoidWhen: The score is smooth and a slope is available; gradient descent finds the minimum with far fewer evaluations.
Each evaluation is slow and the budget is a few dozen runs; Bayesian optimization learns from every run, whereas annealing needs thousands of tries.

example.scenario: A researcher tunes a mean-reversion rule on MNQ 5-minute bars with two settings, a lookback window and a holding time. The score is jumpy, so the search uses annealing with 2,000 tries.

input.summary: The two settings, the starting state and the cooling schedule.

fields.name: lookback window range
fields.meaning: How many past 5-minute bars define the average that price must stretch away from before the rule enters.

fields.name: holding time range
fields.meaning: How many 5-minute bars a trade is held before exit.

fields.name: starting score
fields.meaning: Net result after costs of the starting setting on the tuning folds. One MNQ point is worth 2 US dollars.

fields.name: starting temperature
fields.meaning: High enough to accept most worse moves; it is measured in the same points as the score.

fields.name: cooling rate
fields.meaning: Share of temperature kept at each cooling step.

output.summary: The best setting seen, its score and how often worse moves were accepted.

fields.name: best lookback window
fields.meaning: Window of the best setting seen.

fields.name: best holding time
fields.meaning: Holding time of the best setting seen.

fields.name: worse moves accepted early
fields.meaning: Share accepted while the temperature was high.

fields.name: worse moves accepted late
fields.meaning: Share accepted once the temperature was near zero.

example.reading: The falling acceptance of worse moves, from 31 percent to 2 percent, shows the search moving from wandering to settling. The score of 38 points per day is in-sample, so re-test the setting on later folds. Running the search again from other starting points and landing on similar settings is a good sign.
